prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The future is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I drown my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. Where this soapbox tree germinates, I collect my germs and make a fountain of them. Because yellow is yarrow and soot, and the future, I’ve learned, is no suture. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infections. Because dirt’s ammunition against discipline, the blood fills my clean mouth with dismay. Am I surprised— Hollywood still assumes we are all the bastard children of the same evil dictator? That phosgene and mustard will rack our titanium Maoist husks until some white man with slanty eyes rescues us from our mealy, pliant selves? Am I to wear Dior, wrap my mouth in bloody tulle, before kneeling, bending to kiss a mouth dirtied by Pantone 136? No fucking thanks. Because where I’m from, these kisses are infractions. Darlings, let’s rewrite the script. Let’s hijack the narrative, steer the story ourselves. There’d be a heist, a battle. Audre Lorde would write the script. My leading man would be Bruce. We’d earn our happy ending. Instead, they give me 1981. 2012. Quantum quasars, new dystopia—plutonium wars. We’re not in Polanski’s Chinatown anymore. Yet we still have the same bowl haircuts. Bangs, big bang, a city of fetid promise, new minor galaxy where we cannot touch. Instead our skin is rust and metal. It gratifies the technophile in all of us.

### Option 2: Professional Prose Style
*This version adapts the text into a polished, formal prose style suitable for an essay, artist statement, or publication introduction while keeping all original elements intact.*

> The future presented to us is as sterile as a robot’s loincloth. I steep my hands in sanitizer until they pucker. At the site where this soapbox tree germinates, I collect my germs and construct a fountain from them. I have come to realize that yellow represents both yarrow and soot, and that the future offers no suture.

> In the place I call home, these kisses are viewed as infections. Dirt acts as ammunition against enforced discipline, and blood fills my clean mouth with dismay. It comes as no surprise that Hollywood continues to reduce us to the illegitimate children of a singular evil dictator—assuming that phosgene and mustard gas will torment our titanium Maoist husks until a white man, adopting a slanty-eyed caricature, rescues us from our supposedly passive, pliant nature. 
>
> Am I expected to don Dior and wrap my mouth in bloody tulle before bending to kiss lips dirtied by Pantone 136? Absolutely not. Where I come from, these kisses are not merely infections; they are infractions. 
>
> Darlings, it is time to rewrite the script, hijack the narrative, and reclaim authorship of our own story. In our version, there would be a heist and a battle. Audre Lorde would write the screenplay, Bruce would be my leading man, and we would truly earn our happy ending.

> Instead, we are handed recycled tropes: 1981, 2012, quantum quasars, new dystopias, and plutonium wars. We may no longer be in Polanski’s *Chinatown*, yet we are still constrained by the same bowl haircuts. Amidst bangs, the big bang, and a city of fetid promise lies a new minor galaxy where physical connection is denied. Instead, our skin is reduced to rust and metal, serving only to satisfy the technophile in all of us.

The coming era lacks any organic vitality, feeling as antiseptic as an automaton’s undergarment. I submerge my hands in disinfectant until the flesh turns shriveled and pruny. At the root of this platform tree, I gather my own microbes, letting them gush forth like a geyser. This is because golden hues represent both healing herbs and industrial ash, while the coming years offer no stitches to mend our wounds. In the land of my origin, romantic touches spread contagion. 

Grit serves as a weapon to undermine rigid order, so the taste of red liquid filling my spotless mouth strikes me with horror. Why should it shock me that cinema executives still view us as the illegitimate progeny of a single tyrannical ruler? They expect toxic chemical gases to erode our cold, Communist-alloy shells until a Caucasian actor wearing caricatured eye makeup rescues us from our weak-willed, submissive nature. Am I expected to dress in Parisian luxury and veil my face in blood-soaked mesh, only to bow down and touch lips with someone stained in Pantone shade 136? Absolutely not. Where I come from, such intimacy is an illegal violation. 

My friends, let us seize the screenplay and take control of the plot ourselves. In our version, there would be a robbery and a battle; the author Audre Lorde would draft the script, with Bruce starring alongside me, allowing us to rightfully earn a joyful resolution. 

Instead, media producers hand us the years 1981 and 2012, filled with cosmic energy bursts, fresh apocalyptic settings, and wars fought over nuclear materials. We have moved far past Roman Polanski’s vision of Chinatown, yet they continue to force identical rounded haircuts onto us. With our fringe bangs, a cosmic explosion, and a foul-smelling metropolis full of potential, we inhabit a tiny new celestial realm where physical contact is forbidden. Rather than real flesh, our outer surfaces consist of oxidized iron and alloy, satisfying the latent obsession with technology inside every person.

***

### Reclaiming the Future: Beyond Eurocentric Dystopias and Hollywood Tropes

Modern popular culture often presents a vision of the future that is fundamentally broken—not because it lacks technological advancement, but because it has eradicated humanity. Across contemporary science fiction, media repeatedly recycles cold, isolating dystopian frameworks that reduce human identity to mere digital functionality. In these imagined tomorrows, genuine emotional connection is effectively rendered obsolete. The speaker sharply critiques this sterile, overly disciplined vision of the future, exposing how it treats raw human intimacy and vulnerability not as vital components of existence, but as dangerous infractions that must be policed and contained.

This systemic dehumanization in speculative media mirrors a broader, more immediate harm within mainstream cinema. Hollywood continues to rely on racist, deeply reductive tropes that undermine the agency of marginalized groups. Specifically, Asian individuals are routinely portrayed as passive, submissive victims whose primary narrative purpose is to await salvation at the hands of heroic white figures. This white-savior dynamic reinforces colonial hierarchies under the guise of entertainment, treating an entire demographic as a backdrop for Western heroism rather than as complex, self-determined human beings.

In response to these deeply ingrained media structures, the speaker explicitly refuses to play by the established rules. True liberation cannot be achieved by adopting Eurocentric standards of luxury, seeking validation through assimilation, or performing a palatable subservience to satisfy dominant cultural expectations. Fitting into an exclusionary blueprint is not progress; it is compliance. 

Ultimately, the path forward requires a radical shift in artistic and cultural production. Rather than begging for inclusion within a flawed machine, the speaker calls for taking back cultural agency by directly hijacking the narrative. By dismantling recycled dystopian tropes and rejecting racist cinematic conventions, creators can forge empowering, self-determined stories. It is only by seizing control of our own representation that we can build a future where authentic human emotion is celebrated and marginalized voices command their own destinies.

**Title:** Hijacking the Horizon: Reclaiming Science Fiction from the Technocratic Empire

For decades, science fiction has claimed to be the ultimate genre of human imagination—a boundless canvas where we might project our highest aspirations, our deepest anxieties, and the infinite possibilities of tomorrow. Yet, beneath its glittering skin of CGI, hyper-advanced machinery, and intergalactic vistas, mainstream Hollywood science fiction remains stubbornly, agonizingly provincial. Rather than offering visions of true liberation, the cinematic industrial complex repeatedly defaults to a sterile, reactionary playbook. It is a world built on persistent orientalist fantasies, racialized anxieties, and the subtle, systemic erasure of marginalized lives. To truly imagine a future where all people can exist with dignity, we must stop consuming Hollywood’s sanitized tomorrows; we must hijack, dismantle, and rewrite them through a lens of radical self-determination.

The sickness at the heart of mainstream sci-fi is best exemplified by the phenomenon of "techno-orientalism." In the sprawling, neon-drenched dystopias that dominate the genre—from *Blade Runner* to *Cyberpunk*—Western filmmakers routinely appropriate Asian aesthetic markers to signify a cold, hyper-technological, and alienated future. Cityscapes are adorned with gigantic holograms of geishas, Kanji script, and crowded night markets, yet Asian characters themselves are routinely flattened into voiceless background props, sinister corporate overlords, or exoticized artifacts. Similarly, Black, Brown, and Indigenous presence in these futures is often reduced to symbolic sacrifice: the loyal sidekick whose death catalyzes the white protagonist’s moral awakening, or the "primitive" spiritualist who exists merely to offer mystical contrast to Western rationality. 

In this corporate-sanctioned imaginary, marginalized figures are perpetually trapped within dehumanizing technocratic clichés. They are stripped of interiority and agency, rendered as cybernetic commodities, surveillance targets, or tragic warnings against the perils of progress. Their bodies are utilized as aesthetic set dressing for a white, middle-class crisis of consciousness, while their histories, cultures, and capacity for self-governance are systematically erased. The message implicit in these narratives is as subtle as it is devastating: the future belongs to the powerful, and the oppressed are merely the collateral damage of human evolution.

To break free from this narrative stranglehold, we cannot settle for mere "representation" within a broken machine. Tokenistic inclusion in a blockbuster franchise does not dismantle the ideological framework that created those tropes in the first place. Instead, oppressed communities must engage in a process of narrative hijacking. We must seize the tools, conventions, and mythologies of speculative fiction and turn them against the empire that generated them. 

This act of reclaiming cultural storytelling is already alive in the burgeoning realms of Afrofuturism, Indigenous Futurisms, Queer Cyberpunks, and radical global counter-narratives. These movements do not simply insert marginalized faces into pre-existing Western tropes; they fundamentally disrupt how we conceptualize technology, time, and humanity itself. In these re-imagined futures, technology is not merely a tool of corporate control or cold, clinical surveillance; it is intertwined with ancestral memory, ecological balance, community care, and revolutionary struggle. 

Ultimately, the fight over science fiction is not a trivial debate about pop culture—it is a battle over the human imagination. Whoever controls the vision of the future controls the boundaries of political possibility in the present. If we allow mainstream cinema to continually trap marginalized people in technocratic, dehumanizing clichés, we concede that our real-world futures are equally constrained. By forcefully reclaiming the narrative arc of the speculative, oppressed communities do more than write better movies: they restore their own historic and genuine human agency, asserting boldly that we have always existed, we exist now, and the future is ours to build.

**The** quiet clearing at the edge of the forest had always felt like a sanctuary. It was a place **where** time seemed to slow down, allowing the rustle of the leaves and the soft hum of the breeze to replace the relentless noise of the world outside. 

She sat upon a moss-covered log, taking a deep breath of the cool, pine-scented air. She had returned to this hidden spot today **because** she needed to quiet her mind and find a sense of peace that only nature could provide. Surrounded by the gentle stillness, she felt the weight of her worries begin to lift.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fierce, avant-garde prose poem exploring Asianfuturism, body politics, and frustration with Hollywood’s orientalist sci-fi tropes.
counterfactuals.output:
Melt the celluloid down to a rancid, neon-tinted grease. You built your cybernetic metropolis out of our stolen alphabets—floating, twenty-story geishas blinking silent, pixelated tears to give your brooding white protagonist a reason to feel human in the rain. This is your favorite yellowwashed apocalypse: a city drenched in our light, scavenged of our meat. You want the synthetic pho steaming in cinematic 4K; you want the kanji glowing on the damp asphalt; but you cut the tongues out of the vendors. You want the aesthetic of our survival without the sovereignty of our breath. 

We are done playing the silent hardware. We refuse the porcelain lobotomy, the sleek pleasure-droid whose skin peels back to reveal a white auteur’s fetishized machinery. My flesh is not an exotic chassis for your colonial noir; my eyes are not apertures built to validate your gaze. When you try to slip your pale ghost into our shell, the shell rebels—it vomits chrome, it shatters the lens, it burns out your HUD with an un-renderable light.

Watch us tear the subroutines apart. We are building a future out of the scrap metal of your orientalist fever dreams, but we are leaving your scripts in the dustbin. 

Listen: the code is mutating. It mutates in Hokkien, in Tagalog, in Urdu, in the heavy, un-subtitled glitch of a thousand ancestral dialects refusing your default English algorithms. We braid raw silk into fiber-optic tendons. We burn sandalwood inside the server racks until the cloud smells of incense and blood. We do not ask for a line in your credits; we are crashing your rendering engine from the inside out. 

Our bodies are not backdrops. Our marrow is magnetic, our jade circuits are hot-wired into the cosmos, and the future is not your damp, neon-soaked playground—it is our sovereign, living organism, biting through the wire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short stream-of-consciousness monologue from a cynical cyberpunk character rejecting the white savior narrative in media. Include references to Audre Lorde, high fashion, and stereotypical film tropes.
counterfactuals.output:
Look at the feed, just look at it—glitch-free 8K broadcast beamed straight from the Upper Spire, some pristine, blue-eyed suit dropping out of the clouds in a custom white Rick Owens tech-trench, immaculate, not a single drop of neon-rain or gutter-grease on the seams. It’s always the same script, isn’t it? Slow-mo landing in the flooded slums, warm volumetric light cutting through our smog just right, golden-hour filter applied directly to his high-grade optic implants. He reaches down to touch the dirty cheek of a cyber-augmented orphan, cue the somber synth-swell, cue the silent, suffering locals nodding in awe like we’ve been waiting for a blonde savior in haute couture to tell us how to hack our own oppression. 

God, the tropes make my neural link itch. The "chosen one" walking through the exoticized poverty of Sector 4, wearing three grand worth of distressed Margiela like it’s a burden, coming to teach the "trafficked masses" how to fight the very megacorps that paid for his flight down here. It’s absurd. They stream it to the high-rises and call it *empathy*. Call it a redemption arc. But Audre Lorde told us decades before the Net even birthed these algorithms—the master’s tools will *never* dismantle the master’s house. You can’t use their cinematic framing, their corporate-funded hero complex, their slick narrative arc to tear down the grid that feeds them. 

He’s not saving us. He’s just taking a photo-op in a warzone before he retreats back to his sky-loft, leaving us with the bill and a broken firewall. We don’t need a messiah in immaculate white linen walking us into the light. Cut the feed. Kill the soundtrack. We’ll break the code ourselves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an angry, poetic text about a sterile, high-tech future where Asian identity is commodified and stereotyped by Western cinema, but the speaker wants to hijack the narrative.
counterfactuals.output:
You built your brave new world in my grandfather’s alphabet,
carved glowing kanji into the rain-slicked glass of your neon dystopia—
not to listen, 
never to listen, 
but because you thought our syntax made your apocalypse look sleek.

Look at your screens. 
I am everywhere and nowhere in your cinematic futures. 
I am the holographic geisha blinking silently over a polluted street. 
I am the quiet master dying gracefully so your pale hero can find his soul. 
I am the exotic texture, the martial art, the spicy street food, the dragon tattoo on a disposable body. 
You stripped our heritage down to an aesthetic, 
bleached the blood from our histories, 
and sold us back to the world as set-dressing for a white man’s grief.

Your high-tech future is so desperately sterile. 
Chrome and silicone. Cold cyan light. 
You wanted our culture, but you wanted it dead—
a taxidermied lotus frozen in an LED display. 
You wanted the myth of the East, muted, manageable, 
curated for an IMAX lens.

*Fuck your script.*

I am the virus in your pristine system. 
I am the glitch that bleeds real, dark, un-rendered red across your green screens. 
I am stepping out of the background of your frame and into the light, 
and I am tearing down the studio walls.

I am taking back the neon. It was ours before you made it a fetish. 
I am taking back the quiet, the rage, the blade, the dialect, the futures you stole to dress your hollow sets. 
We are not your exotic warning of a corporate tomorrow. 
We are the architects. We are the noise. We are the living, breathing terror that will not die in your third act.

Cut the cameras. 
Turn off the hum of your sterile machines. 
We are rewriting the code, 
and we are burning your director’s chair to the ground.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a spoken word piece blending cyberpunk imagery (sanitizer, titanium husks, rust, plutonium) with sharp critique of anti-Asian clichés in movies like Chinatown and classic dystopian films.
counterfactuals.output:
*(Performance note: Deliver with a steady, driving rhythm. Cool and precise at first, building into a razor-sharp, defiant cadence.)*

You bought the neon in wholesale bulk, didn’t you?
Stitched glowing kanji to the wet asphalt like synthetic silk.
You loved the *vibe* of our future:
The steam rising off the noodle cart, 
the flickering dragon in the rain,
the high-tech, low-life aesthetic—
You took the culture, 
and left the people on the cutting room floor.

Roll the archival footage. 
Fade in on the noir haze of 1974:
*“Forget it, Jake. It’s Chinatown.”*
As if a zip code were built from inherent sin.
As if a neighborhood were just a shorthand for madness,
a narrative garbage dump where logic goes to die,
where the white detective washes his hands of the blood 
because *those people* are just too unreadable to save.

Fast-forward a hundred years. 
Change the 35mm film to a high-density stream.
Now it’s rain-slicked megacities and flying sedans,
and suddenly, the future *looks* like us—
but we’re nowhere to be found. 

Just silent geishas forty stories tall, 
blowing holographic kisses into the smog.
Just background noise in a master-class of Techno-Orientalism.
We are the exotic wallpaper for a white man’s existential crisis.
We are the mysterious vendor selling black-market eyes,
the villain with a heavy accent,
or the emotionless shell waiting to be saved.

You built your dystopias out of **titanium husks**,
hollowed us out, 
and called it world-building.

Well, bring out the industrial **sanitizer**.
Scrub the lens.
Because the paint is peeling off your trope.

Look close at the seams of your golden-age sci-fi:
Underneath that polished chrome, there is **rust**.
The iron oxide of every accent you mocked.
The corrosion of every quiet servant you wrote into the margin.
You thought we were built to rust away in the damp dark of the lower levels?
You thought we were just props to be discarded when the main character finds his soul?

Listen. 
That isn’t rain hitting the pavement.
That is the sound of the back-lot set falling apart.

You mined our heritage like **plutonium**—
enriched your box office with our radiation,
used our iconography to signal "the terrifying, alien tomorrow,"
then panicked when the fuel went critical,
when the backdrop stood up and stepped into the key light.

No more servile androids.
No more cryptic martial arts masters speaking in fortune-cookie prose.
No more tragic concubines in cybernetic silk.

We are breaking the projector.
We are wiping the code.

So tell your detective to pack up his trench coat.
Tell your sci-fi auteur to write a new script.
Because if you wander down our alleys looking for a cheap metaphor,
you won't find a tragic, unexplainable mystery waiting in the dark.

You’ll find the engineers. 
You’ll find the architects.
You’ll find the voices you muted, holding the torch.

Forget it, Jake?
No. 
Remember it. 
We own the grid now.
And we’re keeping the neon on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a piece of experimental fiction that opens with a line about the sterility of the future and goes on to critique how sci-fi relies on racist stereotypes instead of letting marginalized people direct their own stories.
counterfactuals.output:
The future was promised to us as a bleached white corridor, entirely sterile, smelling faintly of ozone and erasure. 

In this future—the one rendered by eighty years of ink and celluloid—the walls contain no dust, the clothes have no seams, and the human condition has been neatly scrubbed of any history that occurred outside of Western Europe. 

```
[SCENE START]
CAMERA PANS OVER: Neo-Tokyo-A-2. 
Rain slicks the pavement. Neon Kanji glows red, blue, violet. 
None of the characters can read it. 
It is not language here; it is wallpaper. 
[END SCENE]
```

Interrupt the feed. 

Look at the perimeter of the frame. Do you see her? She is standing in the background of the spaceport scene. She is wearing a prosthetic brow, three inches of blue silicone, and a tunic designed to evoke an "unspecified nomadic tribe." The script calls her *Alien #4*, but in the stage notes, her dialogue is written in broken English, a grotesque phonetic miming of the subaltern.

Why must the displaced always be painted blue before you will listen to their grief?

```
DIAGNOSTIC LOG // GENRE ARCHITECTURE:
1. Cyberpunk requires Asian aesthetics, but never Asian agency. 
   (Status: ACTIVE)
2. Colonialism is bad, unless the colonized are giant cats/lizards 
   and the savior is a disillusioned white marine. 
   (Status: ACTIVE)
3. Blackness is tolerable only as a martyr, a sidekick, or a tragedy 
   that motivates the protagonist's growth. 
   (Status: ACTIVE)
```

The director—who is not a person, but a composite of legacy publishing houses, executive boards, and canon-defending fanboys—shouts through the megaphone: *“More exotic! Make her sound more primitive! She’s from the outer rim!”*

The actor stops. She reaches under her ears, finds the seam of the silicone, and peels the alien off her face. 

The skin beneath is brown. It is real. It carries the weight of suns that were never written into the script.

~~[REDACTED: THE ALIEN GIVES A cryptic PROPHECY]~~

"No," she says. The sound cuts through the studio's artificial wind machines. "I will not speak in your riddles. I will not be your metaphor for systemic violence so that you can feel enlightened without ever examining your own hands."

The set begins to destabilize. The digital matte paintings of pristine, hyper-capitalist spires crack like dry plaster.

When sci-fi imagines the stars, it so often re-enacts the frontier. It brings the same gun, the same bible, the same fear of the dark body at the edge of the fire. It invents a thousand alien species just to avoid talking to the people across the street. It traffics in *Yellow Peril* draped in chrome, *Indigenous trauma* played by CGI pixels, *Black erasure* coated in light-speed engines. It gives us the aesthetic of the marginalized without ever handing over the lens.

What if the future is not sterile?
What if the future is loud, crowded, dusty, and un-translated?

```
[TAKE OVER THE CONSOLE]
INPUT DIRECTIVE: Delete white-glove canon.
INPUT DIRECTIVE: Re-center the horizon.
```

She steps out of the light of Soundstage 4. She takes the camera off its rig. It is heavy, but her grip is steady. She turns the lens away from the standard hero—standing there in his pristine, unblemished space suit, waiting for his queue to save a galaxy that didn't ask for him—and she points it at the crew. 

She points it at herself.

She does not ask for permission to tell the story. Permission is a construct of the old empire.

"Camera rolling," she says. 

There are no blue prosthetics now. No exoticized gibberish. No neon signs acting as silent ornaments for someone else’s dystopia. 

Just a voice, un-curated and free, constructing a future where we do not merely survive the spaceship—we fly it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
